title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural purpose of the suspended platform system.
student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended platform system?
instructor: The system supports an equipment load and transfers it through lower rigid member AB, lower wires AH and BC, upper rigid member DC, upper wires ED and FC, and finally into the fixed overhead support.
gradingNotes: Students should describe support and force transfer, not merely identify the assembly as a platform.

title: External Load and Eccentricity
learningObjectives: Explain why payload position affects support-wire forces.
student: Where is the external load applied, and why does its position matter?
instructor: Load P is applied to lower rigid member AB at an eccentric location. Its position controls the moment about the lower-wire attachment points, causing unequal wire forces and unequal elongations that rotate the member.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish fixed anchors from movable rigid members.
student: Identify the supports and boundary constraints in the system.
instructor: The upper ends of wires ED and FC are attached to fixed overhead anchors E and F. Members AB and DC are rigid but are free to translate and rotate as the four tension wires elongate.
commonMistakes: Do not model either horizontal member as a fixed beam.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load through both levels of the suspended assembly.
student: Trace the load path from the equipment load to the building structure.
instructor: Equipment load P → lower rigid member AB → lower wires AH and BC → upper rigid member DC → upper wires ED and FC → fixed overhead support → building structure.

title: Critical Components
learningObjectives: Separate deformable wires from rigid load-distribution members.
student: Which components are most important for the base mechanics analysis, and what role does each play?
instructor: The four wires are deformable axial members and control vertical displacement. Rigid members AB and DC distribute forces and impose displacement compatibility but are assumed not to deform.

title: Mechanical Response and Scope
learningObjectives: Identify the responses supported by the supplied data.
student: Identify the mechanical responses considered for the wires and rigid members in this problem.
instructor: The wires undergo axial tension and elongation. The rigid members undergo small vertical translations and rotations produced by unequal endpoint displacements. Strength failure, fatigue, connector stress, and rigid-member bending are outside the base problem.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect the input variables to equilibrium and axial deformation.
student: Identify the loading, geometric, and material parameters that control displacement and tilt.
instructor: The required inputs are P, Aw, Ew, Lu, Ll, LDC, LAB, xDH, and xP. The remaining upper span is xHC = LDC - xDH = {{platform_x_HC_ft}} ft.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the real assembly into two rigid bodies connected by axial wires.
student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Show the fixed anchors, four vertical wires, rigid members AB and DC, payload location, and symbolic dimensions. Include separate free-body diagrams for both rigid members.
instructor: A correct model has two horizontal rigid members connected by vertical axial tension wires. The upper member is suspended from fixed anchors by ED and FC; the lower member is suspended from the upper member by AH and BC; and concentrated load P acts eccentrically on AB.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor reference idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting equilibrium and compatibility analysis.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the physical system into the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Typical assumptions are rigid members AB and DC; straight, vertical, uniform, linearly elastic wires; axial wire force only; fixed anchors E and F; static loading; small displacement and rotation; ideal pin or eye connections; and neglected wire self-weight and local connection effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the coupled equilibrium and displacement solution.
student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence needed to determine load displacement and member tilt.
instructor: Use equilibrium of AB to find lower-wire forces; use equilibrium of DC to find upper-wire forces; calculate all four wire elongations; interpolate the upper-member displacement at H; add lower-wire elongations to obtain displacements at A and B; interpolate at the load point; then calculate each member's small-angle rotation from its endpoint displacement difference.

title: Boundary Conditions and Unknown Wire Forces
learningObjectives: Interpret the reference idealization and define unknown tensions.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the fixed points, rigid bodies, and four unknown wire forces.
instructor: Ceiling anchors E and F are fixed. AB and DC are rigid bodies. The unknown axial tensions are TED, TFC, TAH, and TBC, each acting vertically along its wire.

title: Equilibrium of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Determine lower-wire forces under eccentric loading.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of lower member AB. For P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}, LAB = {{L_AB}} {{L_AB_unit}}, and xP = {{x_P}} {{x_P_unit}}, determine TAH and TBC.
instructor: For AB, ΣFy = 0 gives TAH + TBC = P. Moments about A give TBCLAB = PxP. Therefore TBC = {{platform_T_BC_lb}} lb and TAH = {{platform_T_AH_lb}} lb.
commonMistakes: The eccentric load does not split equally between the lower wires.

title: Equilibrium of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Transfer lower-wire forces to the upper rigid member and solve support tensions.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of upper member DC and determine TED and TFC. Show where the lower-wire forces act on DC.
instructor: The lower wires apply downward forces TAH at H and TBC at C. Thus TED + TFC = P. Moments about D give TFCLDC = TAHxDH + TBCLDC. Therefore TFC = {{platform_T_FC_lb}} lb and TED = {{platform_T_ED_lb}} lb.

title: Wire Elongations
learningObjectives: Calculate elongation of all four tension wires with consistent units.
student: Calculate the elongation of each wire using δ = FL/(AE). Use Aw = {{A_w}} {{A_w_unit}} and Ew = {{E_w}} {{E_w_unit}}.
instructor:
Use Lu = {{L_u}} ft = {{L_u}}(12) in, Ll = {{L_l}} ft = {{L_l}}(12) in, and Ew = {{E_w}} ksi = {{E_w}}(1000) psi.

δAH = {{platform_delta_AH_in}} in, δBC = {{platform_delta_BC_in}} in, δED = {{platform_delta_ED_in}} in, and δFC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} in.
commonMistakes: Convert feet to inches and ksi to psi when force is in pounds and area is in square inches.

title: Displacement of Point H
learningObjectives: Interpolate displacement along a rigid member undergoing small rotation.
student: Using rigid-body compatibility of upper member DC, determine the downward displacement of point H.
instructor:
Point D moves downward by δED, and C moves downward by δFC. Since H is xDH/LDC of the distance from D to C,

δH = δD + (δC - δD)(xDH/LDC) = {{platform_delta_H_in}} in downward.

title: Endpoint Displacements of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Combine support motion and lower-wire elongation.
student: Determine the downward displacements of endpoints A and B of lower rigid member AB.
instructor: Point A is suspended from moving point H through wire AH, so δA = δH + δAH = {{platform_delta_A_in}} in downward. Point B is suspended from moving point C through wire BC, so δB = δC + δBC = {{platform_delta_B_in}} in downward.
gradingNotes: Both upper-support motion and lower-wire elongation must be included.

title: Vertical Displacement of the Equipment Load
learningObjectives: Determine load-point displacement from endpoint motions.
student: Determine the vertical displacement of the equipment load on lower member AB.
instructor: The load is xP/LAB of the distance from A to B. Therefore δload = δA + (δB - δA)(xP/LAB) = {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward.

title: Tilt of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle rotation of AB.
student: Determine the small-angle tilt magnitude and physical direction of lower member AB.
instructor: |θAB| ≈ |δB - δA|/LAB = {{platform_theta_AB_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_AB_deg}}°. Member AB tilts {{platform_lower_tilt_direction}}.

title: Tilt of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret the small-angle rotation of DC.
student: Determine the small-angle tilt magnitude and physical direction of upper member DC.
instructor: |θDC| ≈ |δC - δD|/LDC = {{platform_theta_DC_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_DC_deg}}°. Member DC tilts {{platform_upper_tilt_direction}}.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Interpret the mechanics results and make a limited recommendation.
student: Identify the wire carrying the largest force and the largest elongation. Use the results to recommend one change that would reduce load displacement or tilt, and state what additional information is needed before service approval.
instructor: Wire {{platform_governing_wire}} carries the largest force, {{platform_governing_force_lb}} lb. Wire {{platform_dominant_wire}} has the largest elongation, {{platform_dominant_elongation_in}} in. The predicted payload displacement is {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward. Increasing wire area or modulus reduces all wire elongations; reducing load eccentricity especially reduces unequal lower-wire elongation and lower-member tilt. Service approval also requires allowable stresses, fatigue requirements, anchor and connector geometry, rigid-member stiffness, tolerances, and applicable facility criteria.
gradingNotes: The recommendation must remain within this deformation model and must not claim that strength or durability has been verified.
